$comment: Why this case is in the corpus: it is the only fragment-selection case that exercises three behaviours
at once. The reply is wrapped in a code fence the prompt explicitly asked it not to use, one entry
carries the knowledge/ prefix the parser has to strip, and the selection both drops a required
fragment and picks up a forbidden one. It is the only case where missing and forbidden come back
non-empty, so a scorer that stopped populating either would still look correct everywhere else.
Over-loading is the failure mode the forbidden metric exists for, and a Maestro fragment in a
Playwright run is the example the harness header names.
The stdout is CONSTRUCTED, for the reason bare-json records.
derivation: The reply opens with a sentence of prose, so parsing the whole text fails. The fenced candidate is
tried first and yields the JSON object, which parses. The reply's fifth entry is
knowledge/selector-resilience.md and the parser strips the prefix, so selection holds seven bare
scoreCase compares that set against the frozen expect block. Of the 7 mustLoad entries the set
contains 6; timing-debugging.md is absent, so missing is [timing-debugging.md] and hits is 7 - 1 = 6.
Of the 3 mustNotLoad entries the set contains maestro-flows.md, so forbidden is [maestro-flows.md] and
forbiddenTotal stays 3. selected is the length of the reply's own list, which is 7.
selector-resilience.md counts as a hit only because the prefix was stripped. Without the strip, missing
would hold two entries and hits would be 5.
The counts the harness derives from these: requiredRecall 6/7 = 0.8571, below the 0.90 floor, and
forbiddenRate 1/3 = 0.3333, above the 0.10 ceiling. Both metrics fail on this one case, which is what
makes it the useful counterweight to bare-json.
